•Legislative Council Policies and Procedures About Harassment

•Harassment Education

•Harassment Reporting

The Policies and Procedures Outline Both Sexual Harassment and Harassment

Sexual Harassment

•Sexual harassment is prohibited under Code section 19B.12. As defined in Code section 19B12, sexual harassment means persistent, repetitive, or highly egregious conduct directed at a specific individual or group of individuals that a reasonable person would interpret as intentional harassment of a sexual nature, taking into consideration the full context in which the conduct occurs, which conduct threatens to impair the ability of a person to perform the duties of employment. Conduct of a sexual nature that interferes with or affects employment decisions regarding an employee, or creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment for an employee, shall constitute unlawful behavior.

Sexual harassment shall include but is not limited to the following:

•Unsolicited sexual advances by a person toward another person who has clearly communicated the other person’s desire not to be the subject of those advances.

•Sexual advances or propositions made by a person having superior authority toward another person within the workplace.

•Instances of offensive sexual remarks or speech or graphic sexual displays directed at a person in the workplace who has clearly communicated objection to that conduct, and where the person is not free to avoid that conduct due to the requirements of employment.

•Dress requirements that bear no relation to the person’s employment responsibilities.

Harassment

In addition to sexual harassment, harassment may include persistent, repetitive, or highly egregious conduct consisting of unwelcome verbal (in-person or by phone, text, email, social media, or any other means) or physical conduct, whether or not based wholly or in part on any characteristic protected by law, directed at a specific individual or group of individuals, that is not justified by a supervisor-subordinate work relationship and that a reasonable person would interpret as designed or perceived to do any of the following:

-Impair the ability of another person in the workplace to perform the duties of employment.

-Threaten, intimidate, or coerce another person in the workplace to act in a manner that is not required by the person’s duties of employment.

-Create an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment.

When It’s not harassment

Courteous, mutually respectful, and non-coercive conduct between employees that is appropriate in the workplace and that a reasonable person would view as acceptable is not considered to be harassment.

According to a study done by the US Merit System Protection Board about Sexual Harassment in the Federal Workplace, victims of sexual harassment have some common characteristics. Which statements do you think are true?? Make your choices by clicking on them and then pushing the submit button to see how you did.

There are four correct responses, more likely to be unmarried, work with individuals of the opposite sex, have attended college, be under the age of 35.

AUDIO: Think of a word or phrase that describes a healthy work environment. Type it on the whiteboard and press Enter. You will need to click the continue button when it appears.

Learner inputs a word

Here are some words that other people who have taken this class have suggested.

Words and phrases fade in (affirming, collaborative, engaging, good communication, helpful, nurturing, opportunity for growth, pleasant, positive, professional, respectful, rewarding, supportive, values diversity)

Now imagine the absence of these qualities. (words and phrases fade out).

Employees and customers who are harassed do not feel their environment has these qualities so sexual harassment can turn a healthy work environment into a poor one. For individuals that experience it, sexual harassment takes its toll in the form of mental and emotional stress and even loss of income, if the victims leave their jobs or take leave without pay as a result of the experience. Workplace sexual harassment is not limited to the confines of an office environment. Any misconduct during a work-related activity such as a company function, corporate event, team building exercise, or out of town business trip can constitute sexual harassment. Click on the continue button.

AUDIO: Sexual harassment is still all too prevalent in the workplace. A recent survey found that 20% of women in the work place have been harassed by a supervisor and 25% by a co-worker, while 6% of men have been harassed by a supervisor and 14% by a co-worker.

As you can see, harassment by a co-worker is more common.

These statistics do not include sexual harassment that goes unreported because of lack of knowledge. According to a report conducted by a EEOC select task force on Harassment in the workplace, roughly three out of four individuals who experienced harassment never even talked to a supervisor, manager, or union representative about the harassing conduct. Employees who experience harassment fail to report the harassing behavior or to file a complaint because they fear disbelief of their claim, inaction on their claim, blame, or social or professional retaliation. Many victims are not aware of the workplace policies regarding sexual harassment that is why training about identifying sexual harassment and strategies to effectively deal with sexual harassment is so important.

As mentioned there are two principle forms of sexual harassment

Quid pro quo

Hostile work environment.

Quid Pro Quo literally means “this for that”. This is usually the most blatant kind of sexual harassment. This occurs when a boss uses a job reward (such as a raise or promotion) or punishment (such as a firing) to force an employee into a sexual relationship. (audio) This type of harassment, which typically involves a harasser who has authority over the victim, is clearly an abuse of power.

Hostile environment harassment is much more subtle then quid pro quo. Employees who claim a hostile environment are arguing that the workplace is so sexually charged that it affects their job performance. (Audio: Stating there is a hostile work environment does not require the employee to experience actual economic loss. Keep in mind it does not necessarily mean that it is a supervisor or person in authority who creates the environment. Coworkers are just as likely as superiors to be the source of hostile environment harassment, and non-employees, may be guilty of creating the offensive environment. It’s important to note, however, that it is the employer who may be held responsible, even though other employees or non-employees may be the source of the harassment.

It is everyone’s responsibility to create a positive work environment. Employees should behave professionally at all times, following the code of conduct set forth by the State of Iowa and the agency. At the same time, managers should set a positive example. Here are some guidelines for everyone to follow:

· Do not operate on assumptions- get to know co-workers as individuals

· Do not tolerate inappropriate jokes or comments

· Avoid unwelcome physical contact with co-workers or customers

· Do not make suggestive comments. The workplace isn’t the place for sexual behavior

· Never use jokes, words or phrases, and gestures with sexual, religious, racial, gender or disability-laden connotation

• Practice courtesy and respect

What do I do if I feel I have been the victim of or a witness to sexual harassment?

According to the US Merit System Protection Board study, the single most common response of employees who are targets of sexually harassing behaviors is to ignore the behavior or do nothing, In fact, going along with the behaviors seems to be about the least effective thing a victim can do. Should discrimination or harassment take place, an employee must take steps to address the problem immediately. According to the same study, the most effective approaches are informal, assertive actions such as informing the harasser that the conduct is unwelcome and must stop or reporting the behavior to someone in a position to help.
Harassment - Reporting Process

Applicability

This policy applies to all central legislative staff agency employees as the alleged harasser or as victims of fellow central legislative staff agency employees. For purposes of this policy, the word “employee” also applies to central legislative staff agency volunteers, interns, and consultants.

Members, employees, interns, and consultants of the Senate and House of Representatives and lobbyists are subject to the jurisdiction of the Senate and House, respectively, regarding harassment complaints.

Victim Reporting Process
If you are the victim of, or you have suspicion of, harassment, there are different reporting requirements based upon the alleged harasser.

1.LSA employee is the alleged harasser.LSA Director or other central legislative staff is the alleged harasser.

2.Member, employee, or a lobbyist of the Senate is the alleged harasser.

3.Member, employee, or a lobbyist of the House is the alleged harasser.

Any complaint may be filed with the Iowa Civil Rights Commission or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Such a complaint is subject to investigation and resolution under time frames established pursuant to federal and state law, which are sufficiently longer than the time frames established by the harassment policy established by the Legislative Council.

LSA Employee is the Alleged Harasser

Reporting Process

•Complete the “Harassment Complaint Form” found in the Legislative Council Policies and Procedures.

•File the complaint with the Director of the LSA.

•The Director shall begin investigation of a complaint within 48 hours of receipt of the complaint, and shall complete the investigation within 30 calendar days. The Director should generally consult with the alleged harasser’s supervisor in the investigation of the complaint.

•If the Director determines that harassment has occurred, the Director shall take appropriate disciplinary action ranging from a written warning or reprimand, to suspension with or without pay, to termination of employment. A Director who neglects to investigate promptly a sexual harassment complaint is also subject to the scope of disciplinary action described in this paragraph, up to and including termination of employment.

LSA Director or Other Central Legislative Staff is the Alleged Harasser

Reporting Process

•Complete the “Harassment Complaint Form” found in the Legislative Council Policies and Procedures.

•If the complaint involves the Director of a central legislative staff agency or an employee of a different central legislative staff agency, the complaint may be filed directly with the Service Committee of the Legislative Council.

•The Service Committee shall begin investigation of a complaint within 48 hours of receipt of the complaint, and shall complete the investigation within 30 calendar days. If the Service Committee determines that harassment has occurred, the Service Committee shall take appropriate action. If the Service Committee neglects to investigate promptly a harassment complaint under this policy, the complaint may be refiled with the Legislative Council, which is subject to the same guidelines as the Service Committee.

Member, Employee, or a Lobbyist of the Senate is the Alleged Harasser

Reporting Process

•Complete the “Harassment Complaint Form” found in the Legislative Council Policies and Procedures.

•If the complaint involves a member or an employee of the Senate or a lobbyist, the complaint should be filed with the Senate in accordance with the Senate harassment complaint or grievance procedures.

•Senate procedures provide that if the complaint involves a Senate employee the complaint shall be filed with the Secretary of the Senate.

-All complaints shall be handled promptly and discreetly by the Senate. The complaining party and the party cited for unwelcome conduct will be notified as to whether action is warranted. If action is not warranted, both parties will be notified of that decision.

-Any person not satisfied with action taken regarding the person’s complaint may continue the process by filing the written complaint with the Rules and Administration Committee.

•Senate procedures provide that if the complaint involves a Senator or Lobbyist, the complaint shall also be filed with the Ethics Committee.

Member, Employee, or a Lobbyist of the House is Alleged Harasser

Reporting process:

•Complete the “Harassment Complaint Form” found in the Legislative Council Policies and Procedures.

•If the complaint involves a member or an employee of the House of Representatives or a lobbyist, the complaint should be filed with the House in accordance with the harassment complaint or grievance procedures established by the House.

•Any employee who believes he or she has been subjected to harassment prohibited by this policy should immediately report that behavior to the employee’s supervisor or to the Chief Clerk. If an employee becomes aware of harassing conduct engaged in or suffered by a House employee, regardless of whether such harassment directly affects that employee, the employee should immediately report that information to the employee’s supervisor or to the Chief Clerk.

•Whenever the Chief Clerk is made aware of a situation that may violate this policy, the Chief Clerk’s Office will conduct a thorough and objective investigation of any harassment claims. If it is determined that prohibited harassment has occurred, appropriate action will be taken against any person found to have engaged in prohibited harassment. A determination regarding the alleged harassment will be made and communicated to the person claiming harassment as soon as practical. The type of discipline administered will be dependent upon the severity of the conduct, as well as any other factors presented in the particular circumstances. Employees violating this policy are subject to discipline, up to and including termination.

Confidentiality and Retaliation

•Any complaint or investigation of harassment shall be handled confidentially.

•There shall be no discrimination or retaliation against an individual who files a complaint or who aids another individual in filing a complaint.

•An employee who has reason to believe that he or she has been retaliated against because of participation in an investigation of a discrimination complaint may file a complaint under the Legislative Council’s harassment policy alleging violation of the probabilities of retaliation, intimidation, or reprisal for assisting in the investigation of a harassment complaint or may also file a charge with the:

-Iowa Civil Rights Commission, or

-U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whichever is appropriate.

If you need to report harassment and you are unclear of the appropriate reporting channel, please consult with your supervisor or the Legislative Human Resources person.

Congratulations in the completion of this training. We hope you have found this information useful and understand that harassment and discrimination will not be tolerated. Supervisors and managers must understand their obligation to be proactive in monitoring workplace behavior as they are often the first line of defense to claims of harassment and discrimination.
